items.title: InnoDB clustered index
items.body: InnoDB stores table rows inside the primary key B-tree, the clustered index. Secondary indexes store the primary key value as their row pointer, so a lookup through a secondary index then traverses the primary key index as well.
items.question: Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys costly in InnoDB?
items.answer: Random keys insert into arbitrary leaf pages, causing page splits, poor locality, and a larger working set in the buffer pool, and every secondary index carries the wide key. Prefer an auto-increment or time-ordered key such as UUIDv7 stored as BINARY(16).

source.name: MySQL Reference Manual - Clustered and Secondary Indexes

items.title: utf8 is not full UTF-8
items.body: MySQL's utf8 character set is an alias for utf8mb3, which stores at most 3 bytes per character and cannot hold emoji or other supplementary characters. Use utf8mb4, which is full UTF-8.

source.name: MySQL Reference Manual - The utf8mb4 Character Set

items.title: Deadlock on insert-if-missing
items.question: Under REPEATABLE READ, two transactions each run SELECT ... WHERE id = 50 FOR UPDATE on a missing row, then both INSERT id 50, and one fails with a deadlock. Why?
items.answer: A locking read on a missing key takes a gap lock. Gap locks do not conflict with each other, so both transactions hold the same gap; each INSERT then waits for the other's gap lock, forming a cycle. Use INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, or rely on the unique key and handle the duplicate-key error.

items.title: REPEATABLE READ vs READ COMMITTED
items.question: Why does InnoDB default to REPEATABLE READ, and why do some teams switch to READ COMMITTED?
items.answer: REPEATABLE READ gives consistent snapshot reads for the whole transaction and historically suited statement-based replication. Its locking reads use next-key and gap locks that can block inserts and cause deadlocks. READ COMMITTED takes far fewer gap locks, which helps write-heavy workloads when row-based binary logging is used.

source.name: MySQL Reference Manual - Transaction Isolation Levels

items.title: Altering a huge table
items.question: You must add a column to a 500-million-row table in production. What do you check before running ALTER TABLE?
items.answer: Whether the change supports ALGORITHM=INSTANT or INPLACE with LOCK=NONE, and state them explicitly so MySQL errors instead of silently copying the table. Also watch the metadata lock: an ALTER waiting behind a long transaction blocks every new query on the table. Online schema change tools help when native DDL cannot.

source.name: MySQL Reference Manual - Online DDL Operations

items.title: Replication is asynchronous
items.body: MySQL replication is asynchronous by default: the source commits without waiting for replicas, so replica reads can be stale and a failover can lose recently committed transactions. Semisynchronous replication narrows that window at a latency cost.
